stalled.intro: Revenue is flat, the team is busy, and nobody agrees on why. More activity is the reflex. It is almost never the answer.
symptoms: Revenue has been flat for three quarters or more.
Everyone has a different theory about the cause.
New initiatives launch, spike, then fade.
The market grew and you did not.
stalled.causes: Stalled growth is rarely one thing. It usually pairs weak demand creation with a conversion journey that leaks, capped by systems that cannot absorb more volume.

examine.why: Pipeline, conversion or capacity: the flat line always starts in one of them.
Half of stall diagnoses collapse when tested against the numbers.
The smallest intervention capable of material change, not the biggest programme.

stalled.proofHeading: Businesses that stalled, and what moved.

conversion.intro: Enquiries arrive and quietly die. The problem is almost never the leads. It is the journey between first contact and decision.
symptoms: Enquiries go quiet after the first reply.
You could not say what your conversion rate is at each step.
Follow-up depends on someone remembering.
Price objections arrive before value was ever shown.
conversion.causes: Conversion problems usually live in the journey, not the leads: slow follow-up, unclear next steps, and an experience that talks people out of buying.

examine.why: Where enquiries actually stall, measured, not assumed.
Response time is the strongest single conversion lever most businesses own.
The gap between what you promise and what an enquiry feels like.

margin.intro: Revenue grows but profit does not. Somewhere between price, mix, cost and manual work, the margin is leaking.
symptoms: Turnover is up and the bank balance is not.
Discounting is the default response to a quiet period.
Prices have not been tested against value in years.
Cost-to-serve creeps up with every workaround.
margin.causes: Margin leaks compound: discounting to create demand, manual work inflating cost-to-serve, and pricing that has never been tested against value.

examine.why: What customers would actually pay, not what feels safe.
Manual work and workarounds that inflate every order.
What each promotion really costs once the uplift is halved.

operations.intro: The team works hard and the business moves slowly. Manual effort is absorbing the capacity growth needs.
symptoms: Key work depends on one person or their spreadsheet.
Hours go on tasks a system should do.
Every sale creates admin somewhere else.
Hiring is the answer to every capacity question.
operations.causes: Operational drag is a scale problem in disguise. Work that depends on effort or memory sets a hard ceiling on how big the business can get.

examine.why: The real workflow, walked through, not the org chart version.
The manual work that automation or better process removes outright.
What stops if one person is away for a fortnight.

demand.intro: The pipeline dries up the moment you stop pushing. Demand depends on effort, not on a system that creates it.
symptoms: New business relies on the same few channels or customers.
Referrals are welcome but unplanned.
Marketing activity spikes and troughs with your attention.
You are invisible where buyers actually look.
demand.causes: Weak demand usually pairs an unclear proposition with channel dependence, and it drags conversion down with it: thin pipelines make every deal feel desperate.

examine.why: Search, referral and repeat: measured against where you show up.
Whether the market can tell what you are for in one pass.
Channels that build an asset versus activity that evaporates.

demand.proofHeading: Demand systems that outlast the campaign.

experience.intro: Customers buy once and drift away. Retention is an experience problem before it is a marketing problem.
symptoms: First-time buyers rarely come back.
Problems surface in reviews, not in conversations.
Repeat rate is a mystery number.
Service quality depends on who is on shift.
experience.causes: Experience leaks show up as conversion and demand problems: replacing lost customers costs more than keeping them ever would.

examine.why: What actually happens between first purchase and the second that never comes.
The gap between marketing and the experienced reality.
Direct feedback, gathered before the review goes public.

ai.intro: Everyone says AI. Almost nobody says where it pays. The question is not which tool, it is which problem.
symptoms: Tools were bought and quietly abandoned.
The team is curious but nobody owns it.
Competitors claim AI and you cannot tell if it is real.
Every vendor pitch starts with the technology.
ai.causes: AI-shaped confusion is usually an operations and scale question: where manual work, decisions or response times are the constraint, AI can pay. Anywhere else it is theatre.

examine.why: AI pays where repetitive judgement and manual work meet volume.
Half of AI ideas die on data quality. Better to know first.
What a tool solves, what needs building, what needs neither.

ai.proofHeading: Practical AI, tested on a real P&L first.

scale.crumb: Systems cannot support the next stage
scale.intro: What got you here creaks at higher volume. Growth is being rationed by spreadsheets, workarounds and heroics.
symptoms: Volume spikes cause errors, not just work.
Reporting takes days and trusts nobody.
Adding revenue means adding headcount at the same rate.
Nobody wants to touch the systems that work.
scale.causes: Scale limits drag operations and erode margin at exactly the moment the business needs both: teams patch by hand what systems should absorb.

examine.why: The workflows that fail at 2x, found before 2x arrives.
Whether numbers exist once, in one place, or many times in many spreadsheets.
What must change first so everything after gets cheaper.

scale.proofHeading: Systems rebuilt ahead of the growth.
